1. FOREWORD
Leaps and bound! Here is a phrase that
comes to mind when we examine the
progress Nigeria has made in safeguarding
the freedoms and interests of data
subjects since the establishment of Nigeria
Data Protection Commission (NDPC) in
2023. The growth trajectory follows the
developmental priorities of the Federal
Government as well as Strategic blueprint
of the Federal Ministry of Communications,
Innovation and Digital Economy. More
importantly, it is a demonstration of our
commitment to the implementation of the
Nigeria Data Protection Strategic Roadmap
and Action Plan (NDPSRAP) 2023-2027.

NIGERIA DATA PROTECTION COMMISSION ANNUAL REPORT 2024 | 9
In the 2024 NDP Report, the reader is invited on a journey of deep reflection
of the Commission in defending Data Sovereignty. Everyone interested
in the development of our economy, the resilience of our security
architecture, and the radiance of our social heritage will appreciate the
effort of the Commission in regulating cross-border data flows. It is, thus,
cheering to note that the Commission is holding data controllers and
processors accountable for their acts and omissions under the Nigeria
Data Protection Act (NDP Act). Similarly, the requirement for fair, lawful
and transparent processing of personal data, rights to information,
access and objection to data processing, which many may esteem
lightly prior to the 4th Industrial Revolution, are now very fundamental to
the work of the Commission. This means that a trader in Ariara, Gusau or
Balogun markets can rest assured that his/her personal data will not be
used to open a bank account or to take a loan without his/her consent.
It is noteworthy that the Commission is keen on leveraging bilateral and
multilateral cooperation in advancing data privacy rights. This can be
observed through its Memoranda of Understanding with Data Protection
Authorities of Canada and Dubai. The Commission’s effort in cooperation
is also evident in its active participation in the Global Privacy Assembly,
which comprises over 130 Data Protection Authorities. Through the
formidable efforts of the Commission, Nigeria won the hosting rights of
the 2025 edition of the Network of African Data Protection Authorities’
Conference and Annual General Meeting, (NADPA-RAPDP). In light of
the foregoing, we can look at 2025 with greater optimism. We have the
enabling law, we have the institution, and, day by day, we are investing in
the people who make both the law and the institution work for the common
good. As it is with every human undertaking, there is room to push the
frontiers of our best endeavours. This is an ecosystem where disruption
takes place at the speed of thought. The 2024 NDP Report demonstrates
that Nigeria is on the right track and is gaining the requisite momentum
for the advancement of data privacy and protection.
DR. VINCENT O. OLATUNJI, CPPPS, CDPO, FIIM
National Commissioner/CEO,
Nigeria Data Protection Commission

3.7 Key Achievements in 2024:
S/N EVENT | FACTS & FIGURES
01 Guideline for Data Controllers & Processors of Major Importance
(DCPMI)
The Guidelines for DCPMI outlines the regulatory framework,
obligations, and best practices applicable to organisations that handle
significant volumes of personal data or operate within critical sectors
of the economy. This document is designed to ensure compliance with
the NDP Act of 2023 and strengthen accountability, transparency, and
data security practices.
02 National Certification Program for Data Protection Officers
The Commission has licensed the Institute of Information Management
(IIM) as the National Certification body for Data Protection Officers. The
certification is aimed at increasing Data Protection Professionals in the
digital ecosystem and maintaining global standards of practice.
03 Responsible Data Management Course (RDMC)
RDMC is a free online course aimed at training 10,000 public servants
within a year. The course aims to foster trust in the public service
ensuring accountability and duty of care when handling data. It equips
Federal and State MDAs with the expertise to manage data securely,
with integrity and mitigate the potential for data-related vulnerabilities
in public service.
04 Issuance of the General Application and Implementation Directive
(GAID)
The Commission has released the GAID, covering 42 areas of data
protection. This guideline includes templates for filling audit returns,
essential principles of data protection, and definitions of key terms not
specified in the NDP Act, 2023.
05 Registration of more Data Protection and Compliance Organisation
(DPCOs)
The registration of DPCOs is a critical component of Nigeria’s data
protection framework, as established under the NDP Act. DPCOs play
a vital role in supporting compliance with data protection regulations

NIGERIA DATA PROTECTION COMMISSION ANNUAL REPORT 2024 | 13
by offering professional advise, compliance, and audit services to Data
Controllers and Processors across the country. NDPC has licensed 246
DPCOs till date.
06 Registration of Data Controllers and Processors of Major Importance
(DCPMI)
The Registration of DCPMI is a regulatory requirement under the
NDP Act, 2023. It mandates organisations that process significant
volumes of personal data or operate in critical sectors to register
with the Commission. This process ensures oversight, accountability,
and compliance with data protection standards. 36,052 DCPMI have
registered so far.
07 Cooperation and Collaboration
The Commission has successfully established Memorandum of
Understanding (MoU) with key partners, which includes:
1. Federal Ministry of Youth Development
2. Huawei Technologies
3. Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada (OPCC)
4. National Insurance Commission (NAICOM)
5. Dubai International Financial Centre Authority (DIFCA)
6. Social media influencer, Enioluwa Adeoluwa.
08 Enhanced Awareness
Over 10,467 events and awareness initiatives have been successfully
conducted across the country, reaching a broad audience through a
diverse range of channels, including radio, television, print media, and
online platforms. These efforts have played a key role in educating the
public about the importance of data protection and their rights under
the NDP Act.

3.8 Synoptic Analysis of the Nigeria Data Protection
Strategic Roadmap and Action Plan (NDP-SRAP) 2023-2027
Introduction
Although, the NDP SRAP was formally launched in 2023, some of its fundamental
initiatives particularly under Governance, Ecosystem and Technology pillars, have
been part of the Commission work in progress since February 2022, when the
Nigeria Data Bureau was established.
NDP-SRAP was meticulously crafted to among others:
a. Define effective strategies to safeguard fundamental rights and freedoms
b. Stimulate lawful use of personal data for national development
c. Identify sustainable initiatives for:
• Developing human capital
• Resourcing the Commission
• Nurturing a vibrant data protection ecosystem
• Collaborating and cooperating with relevant institutions and persons
To this end, the drafters, through a painstaking process of policy development
(including research, consultation and validation workshops) set forth 5 strategic
pillars upon which the regulatory functions of the Commission rest. The Pillars are:
• Governance
• Ecosystem and Technology
• Human Capital Development
• Cooperation and Collaboration
• Funding and Sustainability
The pillars are covered extensively in the NDP-SRAP document. Our task is to pen
a synoptic analysis of the NDP-SRAP implementation. Our focus will be on People,
Process and Technology.
People:

developed. These are:

Thus, in implementing NDP-SRAP, the Commission prioritises initiatives that
would have the most significant impact on the largest possible scale. In creating
awareness among data subjects, considering the sheer size, the Commission
seeks collaboration with public-minded persons and institutions. The Commission’s
initiative on privacy clubs in schools is a good example. Similarly, the Commission is
partnering with reputable organisation to train and certify Data Protection Officers.
The DPOs are central in connecting people (data subjects) to data controllers and
processors. The Commission is currently sponsoring the training and certification
of 500 Data Protection Officers.
Process
With the staggering data on People in mind, the process being adopted to serve
them must of necessity be democratic and agile. This aspect speaks to the
governance pillar particularly. At the moment, there are 9 (nine) major procedures,
namely:
a. Complaints Investigation and Resolution
b. NDP Act Compliance Audit Returns Filing
c. Registration of Data Controllers and Processors of Major Importance
d. Registration of Data Protection Compliance Organisations
e. Human Capital Development
f. Cooperation and Collaboration
g. Sandboxing
h. Data Privacy Impact Assessment
i. Rule Making
The processes are evolving even as the paradigm of data governance shifts in
response to the dictates of people and technology. Nonetheless, the Constitution
of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the NDP Act serve as the anchor and sails of
data privacy and protection.
Technology
NDP-SRAP accords priority to technology. This is evident in the second Pillar which
is Ecosystem and Technology. In order to serve the people and make the processes
more effective, some technological solutions have been adopted and others are
being considered for adoption. The Commission for instance relies on Enterprise
Resource Planning (ERP) which helps in automation of critical processes within the
Commission. Similarly, the Commission has created service portal to handle:
• Complaints
• Enquiries
• NDP Act Compliance Audit Filing

• Registration for Training and Participation in the Commission’s Events, Etc
The next phase of technology adoption focuses on the use of Emerging
Technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning to
create awareness, strengthen data security and facilitate smooth resolution of
complaints.

4. KEY INITIATIVES
4.1 Awareness & Capacity Building
In 2024, the Commission intensified its efforts to build capacity and foster a culture
of data privacy and protection. Recognising the evolving challenges in the digital
landscape, the Commission conducted a comprehensive needs assessment
to identify gaps in knowledge, skills, and resources among stakeholders. This
assessment informed the design of targeted capacity-building programs tailored
to address specific needs across various sectors.
Key areas identified included limited awareness of data protection laws, inadequate
technical expertise for compliance, and insufficient understanding of emerging
cybersecurity threats. Armed with these insights, the Commission developed
and implemented a series of training programs, workshops, and stakeholder
engagements aimed at addressing these critical gaps.

4.2 National Certification Program Pilot Testing (DPOs)
The NDPC has made significant strides in strengthening data protection and
privacy with a pilot testing of the National Certification Program. This initiative aims
to certify individuals that have a keen interest in the data protection ecosystem as
Certified Data Protection Officers (CDPOs). It represents a proactive step toward
aligning the country with global best practices, such as the EU’s General Data
Protection Regulation (GDPR), while addressing Nigeria’s unique socio-economic
and technological landscape.
The pilot test involved a cross-section of participants from different sectors and
MDAs who underwent rigorous assessments to demonstrate knowledge of the
core principles of data protection and privacy as enshrined in the Nigeria Data
Protection Act (NDP Act) and other related frameworks.
The outcomes of the pilot were promising. It highlighted areas requiring further
clarity and refinement, such as the scalability of certification tools and the need for
increased public education.
This initiative positions Nigeria as a leader in Africa’s data protection landscape by
promoting awareness, bridging the skills gap, fostering trust in digital systems and
safeguarding the privacy rights of its citizens.
4.3 Responsible Data Management Course (RDMC)
The Commission in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Communications,
Innovation and Digital Economy and Data.org launched a Responsible Data
Management Course to create awareness and capacity building about data
privacy and protection in Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs). This
includes, educating public servants about responsible data management and how
this relates to accountability and the duty of care towards the public that they serve.
The RDMC is a free online course aimed at training 10,000 public servants within
a year. The course aims to foster trust in the public service ensuring accountability
and duty of care when handling data. It equips Federal and State MDAs with the
expertise to manage data securely, with integrity, and mitigate the potential for
data-related vulnerabilities in public service. Certificates would be issued freely to
participants after successful completion of the course.
4.4 Network of African Data Protection Authorities
Conference and AGM (NADPA-RAPDP 2025)
The selection of the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) to host the 2025
Network of African Data Protection Authorities (NADPA-RAPDP) Conference and
AGM marks a significant achievement in the Commission’s mission to lead data

NIGERIA DATA PROTECTION COMMISSION ANNUAL REPORT 2024 | 21
protection efforts across Africa. This prestigious responsibility underscores NDPC’s
commitment to advancing data privacy, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and
enhancing data protection capabilities in the face of an evolving digital landscape.
Hosting the NADPA conference offers Nigeria a prime opportunity to highlight its
progress in data protection and provide a collaborative platform for African Data
Protection Authorities to exchange knowledge. The conference will address
critical issues such as cross-border data flows, privacy laws, digital economy,
artificial intelligence, and digital innovation—key topics in the continent’s ongoing
digital transformation.
This milestone further solidifies Nigeria’s dedication to promoting ethical and lawful
data practices, while reinforcing NDPC’s pivotal role in shaping data governance
standards that protect citizens’ rights. As the host, NDPC is poised to foster valuable
partnerships and influence policy developments that will strengthen Africa’s data
privacy framework.
4.5 Establishment of Data Privacy Clubs at Tertiary
Institutions
In 2024, the Commission initiated the establishment of Data Privacy Clubs in
tertiary institutions to promote a culture of data protection and privacy awareness
among students. These clubs serve as hubs for learning, advocacy, and peer-to-
peer engagement, equipping students with the knowledge and skills to uphold
data privacy principles both within their academic environments and in their future
careers.
By partnering with educational institutions, the Commission facilitated the creation
of platforms where students could actively engage in discussions, training
sessions, and initiatives focused on privacy rights, data security, and compliance
with data protection laws. This initiative underscores the Commission’s dedication
to nurturing a generation of privacy-conscious individuals who will drive a secure
and responsible digital future. The Data Privacy Clubs represent a strategic step in
fostering widespread awareness and embedding data protection as a core value
in academic and professional spaces.
4.6 Training 5,000 Youths in Data Protection and Privacy
The Commission in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Youth Development,
plan to launch an initiative to train 5,000 youths across Nigeria in Data Protection
and Privacy. This initiative aims to equip the youths with the necessary skills and
knowledge to navigate the Nigeria Data Protection Act and foster a culture of privacy
rights in the digital age. This initiative represents a significant step towards building

a more privacy-conscious society in Nigeria through education and engagement
of youths.
The target objectives of the training includes but not limited to:
• Promoting career opportunities in data protection compliance and security.
• Improving the overall digital literacy of all youths.
• Equipping young individuals with an understanding of the data protection
laws and practices.
• Enabling the youths to advocate for data protection in their various
communities and increasing awareness about safeguarding personal data.
• Promoting inclusivity among diverse groups of youths and accessibility to
disadvantaged communities.
4.7 NDPC International Journal of Data Privacy and
Protection
As part of its mission to advance data governance and privacy standards, the
Commission announced the Call for Papers (CFP) for its inaugural International
Journal of Data Privacy and Protection.
This journal is a strategic initiative aimed at promoting comprehensive research,
informed dialogue, creating awareness, knowledge-sharing, and promoting
international best practices in the area of data protection and privacy. The journal
provides a platform for data protection and privacy experts, researchers and
professionals to present research and development in form of articles, notes, book
reviews, among others.
Submissions were welcomed from researchers, academics, policy analysts, legal
practitioners, and industry experts who contributed original research and analysis
on key topics in this evolving field. These submissions underwent a rigorous peer-
review process and were evaluated based on originality, depth, accuracy, and
relevance to the focus and scope of the CFP.

5. REGULATORY ACTIONS
5.1 Issuance of NDP Act General Application and
Implementation Directive (GAID)
The issuance of GAID is a regulatory milestone, not least because it provides more
safeguards for data subjects’ rights but it also promotes the lawful use of data for
public good.
Perhaps the most exciting feature of GAID is the democratisation of the complaints
process. This is referred to as Data Subject’s Standard Notice to Address
Grievance (SNAG). Data Subject SNAG is a tool which enables a data subject in
Nigeria (regardless of their location anywhere in the world) to enforce his data
subject right through the instrumentality of law and technology. The Commission
is already working on integrating Data Subject SNAG on its service portal and it will
be available online within the First Quarter of 2025.
5.2 Investigation and Enforcement Actions
Investigation and Enforcement are central to the regulatory actions of the
Commission. The Commission is currently investigating 213 cases of alleged
violations of privacy rights in the following sectors: health, telecommunications,
banking/fintech and hospitality.
Noting that the obligations imposed under the NDP Act are considered as emerging
legal norms in data governance, the approach adopted by the Commission in
investigation and enforcement is restorative justice as against punitive justice. This
approach finds support in the following provisions of the NDP Act, among others:
• Sections 46(7) – making representations on behalf of parties.
• 47(2)(a)-(c) – issuing warnings and non-penal compliance orders.
• 48(2)(d) – ordering the payment of remedial fees in lieu of strict penalties.
• 48(6) - evaluating extenuating factors such as minimal degree of impact on
privacy and cooperation with the Commission for the purposes of amicable
resolution.

2. Behavioural Profiling This is one of the pitfalls in big data advertisement
and revenue drive. While it may appear desirable
that data subjects only get to see what is of interest
to them, it is disturbing to note that in many cases
this process notoriously violates the the principles of
data minimisation. What is more, profiling may lead
to socio-political manipulation of a large populace.

3. Unauthorised Access to This type of breach take many forms, the less sinister
Personal Data being careless viewing by an unathorised employee
of a data controller or processor. The real malicious
access comes with criminal intent. Reporting
breaches has been a grey area – perhaps due to
fear of retribution. Some data controllers believe
that they can arbitrarily dismiss reportable breaches
as insignificant. However, experience teaches that
reporting breaches and informing data subjects
timeously helps in disaster recovery.
8 Steps for Data Breach Response and Investigation |
Syteca by Liudmyla Pryimenko
4. Loss of Personal Data Nothing demonstrates poor data management
more than the loss of personal data. For a data
subject, the experience may be traumatic. There
was an instance where the data subject required the
personal data to resolve a serious financial scandal.
In another instance, it was meant to complete a
crucial ID. The Commission views personal data
loss with grave concern. Apart from the agony
of replacing lost data, the financial implication
for individuals and businesses is overwhelming.
According to a report titled What is the Cost of Data
Loss in 2024? Invenio IT by Tracy Rock, published by
Invenio IT:

26 | NIGERIA DATA PROTECTION COMMISSION ANNUAL REPORT 2024
• 2022 study by IBM and Ponemon Institute found
that the global average cost of a data breach was
a staggering $4.35 million, or approximately $164
per data record. However, that research mostly
focused on the costs of data breaches, such as
theft of personal user data, login information and
credit card numbers.
• A leading BC/DR provider estimated that a data
loss costs U.S. businesses an average of $7,900
per minute during a datacenter outage.
A recent report by Verizon found that “small”
instances of data loss (around 100 lost or
compromised records) cost businesses an average
of $18,120 to $35,730.
• The same study found that large-scale data loss

Safeguarding Nigeria’s Children in the Digital Age
- Ridwan Oloyede
Introduction
The digital revolution has profoundly transformed how children learn, socialise,
and interact with the world. While offering unprecedented opportunities, the
online environment also presents significant risks to their safety and privacy.
Children are particularly vulnerable to various online harm, ranging from exposure
to inappropriate content and cyberbullying to more insidious threats with data
protection implications. This necessitates a robust legal and regulatory framework
to safeguard children in Nigeria’s evolving digital landscape. This article analyses
the Nigerian Data Protection Act (NDP Act) and its safeguards for protecting
children online. It examines how it strengthens the previous Nigeria Data Protection
Regulation (NDPR) and provides functional recommendations for a safer digital
future for children.
Challenges, Risks, and Harms
The online environment presents a complex web of risks for children, manifesting
in various forms, each posing unique challenges. For instance, children can easily
encounter sexually suggestive material, violent content, or hate speech online, all
of which can have detrimental psychological and emotional effects.1 Furthermore,
the virtual space can become a breeding ground for cyberbullying, harassment,
and intimidation, causing significant distress and impacting children’s mental
health.2 This vulnerability is further compounded by the risk of online grooming
and exploitation, where predatory individuals may use these platforms to befriend
children, gain their trust, and ultimately exploit them for sexual purposes.3
Beyond these direct harms, children also face data security and privacy risks. Their
data, if compromised through data breaches, can lead to identity theft, financial
fraud, and other forms of exploitation.4 Even without breaches, the collection,
use, and sharing of children’s data without safeguards can infringe on their data

The NDP Act and its Safeguards for Children
The NDP Act represents a significant step forward in protecting children’s data in
Nigeria, building upon the foundation laid by the NDPR and introducing several key
enhancements. The NDP Act specifically addresses the processing of children’s
data, incorporating crucial safeguards.16 Firstly, where consent is the appropriate
lawful basis for processing a child’s data, the NDP Act mandates obtaining parental
or guardian consent before such processing occurs, aligning with the principle
of parental responsibility.17 This requirement strengthens the NDPR by providing
a clearer legal basis for processing children’s data. Notably, while the NDPR
Implementation Framework stipulated under 13 years as the relevant age,18 the
NDP Act now defers to the Child Rights Act, which defines a child as anyone under
18, thus providing much-needed clarity and consistency.19
Secondly, the NDP Act requires data controllers to implement “appropriate
mechanisms” to verify age and consent, taking into consideration available
technology.20 While the Act suggests government-approved identification
documents as one possible verification mechanism,21 it also acknowledges the
need for flexibility and other suitable methods. This provision addresses a critical
gap in the previous framework, promoting more robust age verification.
Thirdly, the NDP Act outlines specific exceptions to the consent requirement.22
These exceptions include processing necessary to protect the child’s vital interests,
processing for education, medical, or social care undertaken by a professional with
a confidentiality duty, or processing for court proceedings. These exceptions are
carefully defined to balance the need for protection with other legitimate interests.
Fourthly, in the processing of data of children aged 13 and above, the NDP Act
empowers the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) to make regulations
specifically for those children.23 This provision recognises the evolving capacities
of older children and allows for a more nuanced approach to data protection.
Finally, to ensure comprehensive protection, the NDP Act explicitly states that its
provisions must be interpreted consistently with the Child’s Rights Act, reinforcing
the commitment to upholding children’s rights.24
Beyond these child-specific provisions, the NDP Act’s general data protection
principles collectively provide crucial safeguards for children by ensuring lawful,
fair, secure, and responsible data processing. The NDPR25 and its Implementation

Complementary Legal Frameworks and Initiatives
The NDP Act operates within a broader legal and regulatory framework. While
the Cybercrimes Act criminalises online offences against children, such as child
pornography, grooming, cyberbullying, and cyberstalking, providing crucial criminal
law protections,28 conventional criminal laws like the Penal Code, the Criminal
Code, and the Criminal Laws of various states also apply where traditional crimes
intersect with children online. The Child’s Rights Act provides a comprehensive
framework for children’s rights, including the right to privacy, further strengthening
the legal safeguards.29 Various initiatives also contribute to child online protection.
The Nigerian Communications Commission is developing a Standard Procedure
for Child Online Protection.30 The NDPC’s ongoing efforts to promote child online
safety include practical action such as conducting awareness campaigns and
actively participating in forums like the Child Online Safety Protection and Reporting
of Abuse.31 These collaborative efforts are essential for addressing the complex
challenges of online safety.
Enhancing Child Online Protection
To further strengthen child online protection in Nigeria, the following
recommendations are proposed:
• Guidance for Data Controllers: Providing clear and detailed guidance for data
controllers on implementing the NDP Act’s child-specific provisions, including
best practices for age verification, consent management, and data processing,
would greatly assist in ensuring compliance and effective protection. For
example, developing interactive flowcharts outlining consent procedures for
different age groups for website operators implementing children’s online
accounts.

• Educational Resources and Awareness: The development and promotion
of age-appropriate educational resources, such as online safety tips and
interactive tools, are crucial for empowering children and their parents with
knowledge about online risks and best practices. For example, creating
animated videos explaining online privacy in simple terms for primary school
children or developing interactive quizzes or games for teenagers on identifying
phishing scams.
• Multi-Stakeholder Collaboration: Enhanced collaboration between relevant
regulatory bodies, academia, law enforcement agencies, civil society
organisations, and the private sector is essential for creating a coordinated and
effective approach to child online protection. For example, collaboration with
the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission could address
deceptive design practices on websites targeting children, which undermine
their autonomy and decision-making.
• Capacity Enhancement: Investing in capacity-building initiatives for relevant
stakeholders, including law enforcement officers, educators, and others
involved in child protection, on child online safety issues, data protection
principles, and effective enforcement strategies would strengthen the overall
protection framework. For example, conducting workshops for teachers on
integrating online safety lessons into the curriculum or providing training for
law enforcement on investigating cybercrimes against children.
• Accessible Reporting Mechanisms: Establishing readily accessible reporting
mechanisms, such as a dedicated help desk or online portal, would empower
children and parents to report online harms and seek timely assistance. For
example, creating a dedicated hotline and online reporting platform for children
to report cyberbullying, online grooming, or exposure to harmful content.
• Digital Literacy Initiatives: Implementing comprehensive digital literacy
programmes for children, parents, and educators is vital for raising awareness
of online risks, promoting responsible online behaviour, and empowering
individuals to use technology safely and effectively. For example, launching
nationwide awareness campaigns through schools, community centres,
and online platforms, using diverse media like social media campaigns, radio
jingles, and TV adverts.
• Addressing Technological Advancements: Proactive consideration of the
risks associated with emerging technologies, such as AI, and the development
of appropriate safeguards are necessary to protect children from potential
future harm. For example, conducting research on the potential impact of AI-
powered chatbots on children’s mental health and developing guidelines for
their responsible use in educational settings.
• International Collaboration and Best Practices: Fostering international
cooperation to address online crimes against children, including sharing best
practices and coordinating enforcement efforts, is crucial for effective global

protection. For example, participating in international working groups on
child online protection and collaborating with international law enforcement
agencies on cross-border investigations of online child sexual exploitation.
• Regular Legal Framework Review: Regular review and updating of the
legal framework are essential to ensure its effectiveness in the face of rapid
technological advancements and evolving online risks. For example, a multi-
stakeholder committee should be established to periodically review the NDP
Act and related legislation to identify areas for improvement and adaptation to
new technological challenges.
Conclusion
The digital space is the new frontier for our children, a space brimming with
opportunity but also perilous. Safeguarding children in this environment is not
just about addressing current threats; it is about investing in their future. This is
not merely a desirable goal but an urgent fundamental responsibility. While the
NDP Act marks a significant step forward in Nigeria’s efforts to protect children’s
data and promote online safety, legislation alone is insufficient. Its true power
lies in its implementation and the collective action it inspires. The onus is on all
stakeholders to translate these legal provisions into tangible protections. Nigeria
can forge a truly safer and more secure online environment for its children by
diligently implementing the recommendations outlined in this article and fostering
robust collaboration among all stakeholders—from government and regulators
to parents, educators, and the tech industry. This demands continuous vigilance,
proactive measures, and an unwavering commitment to upholding children’s
rights, ensuring they can reap the immense benefits of the digital world without
sacrificing their safety, privacy, and well-being.
